verbatim_context:
SSI (Supplemental Security Income)
  This is often the most relevant program for someone younger with low income and limited assets. She can work part time and still receive SSI as long as:
  - Her medical condition meets Social Security’s disability standard.
  - Her monthly earnings remain low enough.
  - Her assets stay under SSI limits (generally $2,000 for one person, excluding some items like one vehicle and personal belongings).

  SSI benefits are reduced gradually as earnings increase rather than stopping immediately. Many people on SSI work part time.

  SSI also usually connects to Medicaid eligibility in New Jersey.

specific_claim: Based on prior work history and payroll tax contributions; includes Trial Work Period; Social Security assesses Substantial Gainful Activity (SGA) limits
verbatim_context:
SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance)
  SSDI is based on prior work history and payroll tax contributions. A 28-year-old may qualify if she worked enough in recent years before becoming disabled.

  She can still work part time while applying, but there are income limits. Social Security looks at whether she is performing “substantial gainful activity” (SGA). If earnings are above the SGA level, Social Security may decide she is not disabled under their rules.

  If approved for SSDI:
  - She can later use work incentive programs.
  - There is a Trial Work Period allowing people to test returning to work without immediately losing benefits.
  - Medicare eligibility eventually becomes available after a waiting period.

specific_claim: Can work part time and still receive SSI; assets limit generally $2,000 for one person; often connects to Medicaid in New Jersey
verbatim_context:
SSI (Supplemental Security Income)
  This is often the most relevant program for someone younger with low income and limited assets. She can work part time and still receive SSI as long as:
  - Her medical condition meets Social Security’s disability standard.
  - Her monthly earnings remain low enough.
  - Her assets stay under SSI limits (generally $2,000 for one person, excluding some items like one vehicle and personal belongings).

  SSI benefits are reduced gradually as earnings increase rather than stopping immediately. Many people on SSI work part time.

  SSI also usually connects to Medicaid eligibility in New Jersey.

specific_claim: Based on prior work history; Trial Work Period and SGA rules apply; Medicare eligibility after waiting period
verbatim_context:
SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance)
  SSDI is based on prior work history and payroll tax contributions. A 28-year-old may qualify if she worked enough in recent years before becoming disabled.

  She can still work part time while applying, but there are income limits. Social Security looks at whether she is performing “substantial gainful activity” (SGA). If earnings are above the SGA level, Social Security may decide she is not disabled under their rules.

  If approved for SSDI:
  - She can later use work incentive programs.
  - There is a Trial Work Period allowing people to test returning to work without immediately losing benefits.
  - Medicare eligibility eventually becomes available after a waiting period.

SSI (Supplemental Security Income)
  This is often the most relevant program for someone younger with low income and limited assets. She can work part time and still receive SSI as long as:
  - Her medical condition meets Social Security’s disability standard.
  - Her monthly earnings remain low enough.

specific_claim: Based on prior work and payroll tax contributions; has SGA income limit; includes Trial Work Period and eventual Medicare after waiting period

SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance)
  SSDI is based on prior work history and payroll tax contributions. A 28-year-old may qualify if she worked enough in recent years before becoming disabled.

  She can still work part time while applying, but there are income limits. Social Security looks at whether she is performing “substantial gainful activity” (SGA). If earnings are above the SGA level, Social Security may decide she is not disabled under their rules.

  If approved for SSDI:
  - She can later use work incentive programs.
  - There is a Trial Work Period allowing people to test returning to work without immediately losing benefits.
  - Medicare eligibility eventually becomes available after a waiting period.

specific_claim: Based on prior work history and payroll tax contributions; can work part time during application but earnings above SGA may disqualify; includes Trial Work Period and eventual Medicare eligibility after waiting period
verbatim_context:
SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance)
  SSDI is based on prior work history and payroll tax contributions. A 28-year-old may qualify if she worked enough in recent years before becoming disabled.

  She can still work part time while applying, but there are income limits. Social Security looks at whether she is performing “substantial gainful activity” (SGA). If earnings are above the SGA level, Social Security may decide she is not disabled under their rules.

  If approved for SSDI:
  - She can later use work incentive programs.
  - There is a Trial Work Period allowing people to test returning to work without immediately losing benefits.
  - Medicare eligibility eventually becomes available after a waiting period.

  If she is still able to work part time, eligibility depends on whether a doctor certifies reduced work capacity and whether she recently paid into NJ payroll disability taxes.

  It is not a long-term disability program.
